keep: The idea is named in one line up front: the pump settles where the head it gives equals the head the pipe needs, the crossing of its curve and the system curve, and a closing valve slides that crossing to less flow and more head.

The rule is stated in words and worked with real numbers from the brief's example: 30 − 0.04q² = 10 + 0.06q² gives about 14.1 L/s at 22 m; friction ×2 gives about 11.2 L/s at 25 m. It is tied to Linear systems' crossing point.
The causal step for why the pump stays at the crossing is given: spare head is an unbalanced push that speeds the water, a shortfall slows it.

The puzzle is answered from the rule: flow falls by about a fifth while head rises by about a seventh, so ρgQH falls from about 3.13 kW to 2.81 kW, with the cited facts that power is near its least at a shut valve and current rises with flow.

The picture is the brief's: valve, speed and suction tank level, an efficiency hump, NPSH bars that turn red with bubbles at the impeller, and a switch to a near-upright positive displacement curve. It includes settings where the cause does not give the effect: 55% speed with no flow, and the positive displacement pump whose flow barely moves.

The brief's one listed lesson-8 mistake, expecting a closed valve to stop a positive displacement pump's flow as it does a centrifugal's, has its own DO screen and hint (screen 12). Other DO screens catch a pump giving its rated flow whatever the pipe, a choked pump loading its motor harder, flow going with speed despite a lift, and fighting cavitation with speed or a throttled suction.

Uncited textbook facts (cool water boiling at low pressure, the pump laws, why a positive displacement pump needs a relief valve, a pump chosen near its best efficiency) are each marked 'textbooks add', and the vapour pressure is an example figure, as the brief's gaps say.
fix: Causal step skipped: why a centrifugal pump's head falls as its flow rises is never given. Add, as a textbook fact, that the impeller's blade shape and the losses inside the pump take more as the flow grows.
The misconception is not shown failing in the explanation: say that many expect a choked pump to work harder, and that it does less.

Unclear sentence on NPSH available ('That means the atmosphere on the tank ...'): state what the suction offers in one plain sentence, including the boiling pressure it loses, then that it must stay above what the pump needs.
False absolute: 'it pits the impeller' and 'All its shaft power goes into the trapped water' are stronger than true. Say it can pit the impeller, and nearly all the shaft power.
The analogy's 'the charger then does less work each second' is not true of its output power in general. Say it draws less from its own supply, which goes with the current it gives.
Screen 13 distractor 'a discharge pipe has started to leak' is muddy, since a meter after the leak would also read less. Use 'a discharge valve has been opened further'. Screen 4 typo: 'What happen'.
The pump laws are not tied back to Powers and roots, where Dan met power going with speed cubed. Name it in the practice.
